meta.description: Not Aristotle. Quote Investigator traces this to American writer Elbert Hubbard, whose 1898–1922 essays carry the saying; the tidy modern wording is a later paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is only one way to avoid criticism: do nothing, say nothing, and be nothing'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Aristotle. It traces to American writer Elbert Hubbard (1898–1922); the neat one-sentence version is a later paraphrase.

answer.label: Not Aristotle — actually Elbert Hubbard
answer.authorDates: 1856–1915 · American writer, publisher & founder of the Roycroft community
answer.sourceLine: There is no evidence Aristotle ever wrote this. Quote Investigator ↗ traces the saying to American aphorist Elbert Hubbard, who used it in several forms from his 1898 “Little Journeys” onward. The polished one-sentence version circulating today is a later paraphrase of Hubbard, not a line from any Aristotle text.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “John North Willys,” in Elbert Hubbard’s Selected Writings, Part 2 (1922)
“Little Journeys to the Homes of American Statesmen” (1898)

source.excerpt: Do nothing, say nothing, and be nothing, and you’ll never be criticized.
trail: The earliest strong match is Hubbard’s 1898 “Little Journeys to the Homes of American Statesmen”: “do nothing, say nothing, be nothing—court obscurity,” per Quote Investigator ↗.
By 1908–1909 the compressed form “To escape criticism: Do nothing, say nothing, be nothing” circulated crediting Hubbard’s magazine The Philistine, again per Quote Investigator ↗.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line in its sourced Hubbard quotes: “Do nothing, say nothing, and be nothing, and you’ll never be criticized,” from “John North Willys” (Selected Writings, Part 2, 1922).
Quote Investigator found “no substantive evidence” for any Aristotle ascription.
source.excerptNote: The wording as printed in Hubbard’s “John North Willys” (collected 1922). The circulating “There is only one way to avoid criticism…” sentence is a streamlined paraphrase of Hubbard’s several versions, not a verbatim quotation.

source.rightsNote: The saying originates in Elbert Hubbard’s works published between 1898 and 1922 — all before 1931 and, with Hubbard’s death in 1915, long in the public domain in the United States. The tidy modern one-sentence wording is an anonymous later paraphrase and carries no separate protection.

author.name: Elbert Hubbard
author.heading: About Elbert Hubbard
author.metaLine: 1856–1915 · American writer, publisher & founder of the Roycroft community
author.bio: Elbert Hubbard was an American writer, epigrammist and publisher best known for the essay “A Message to Garcia” and for founding the Roycroft artisan community in East Aurora, New York. Through his magazines The Philistine and The Fra and his “Little Journeys” biographical series, he coined and popularized hundreds of pithy aphorisms. He died aboard the Lusitania in 1915.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The line is endlessly shared as ancient wisdom from Aristotle, but no Aristotelian text contains it — and the specialists who investigated it point to a modern American writer.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ found “no substantive evidence” for an Aristotle ascription; the wording and idiom are modern, not from the Greek corpus.
Hubbard used the saying in several forms — from “Little Journeys” (1898) to “John North Willys” (collected 1922) — and Wikiquote ↗ lists it in his sourced quotes.

The clean “There is only one way to avoid criticism: do nothing, say nothing, and be nothing” sentence does not match any single Hubbard printing verbatim; it is a streamlined composite of his versions.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Elbert Hubbard’s, first printed in 1898 — not Aristotle’s — per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Elbert Hubbard was a machine for aphorisms, and this one mutated as it traveled. His 1898 version was grim and elaborate — “If you would escape moral and physical assassination, do nothing, say nothing, be nothing…” — before newspaper filler columns and his own magazines compressed it into the punchy “To escape criticism: Do nothing, say nothing, be nothing.”

Somewhere in the twentieth century the saying was re-dressed as “Aristotle,” a common fate for tidy maxims that sound timeless. The dignity of an ancient name lends borrowed authority — but the paper trail runs to East Aurora, New York, not ancient Athens.
